cards.def: From Latin for "middle age," the era between Rome's fall and the Renaissance.
The earliest, Germanic form of English, whose words changed endings to show grammar.
The French dialect spoken by England's ruling class after 1066.
English after 1066, with simpler grammar, many French words, and no standard spelling.
The English of Shakespeare, with mostly fixed spelling and near-modern vowel sounds.
A language that changes word endings to show tense, number, or case.
A mournful tone that laments loss and the passing of time.
A bond where the lord gives his warriors treasure and they give him loyalty to the death.
Using a part ("keel") or a related thing ("crown") to stand for the whole thing.
A payment to a victim's family that replaced blood revenge.
The council of nobles that advised Anglo-Saxon kings.
An army of ordinary men called up to defend the kingdom.
The king's official over a county, and the origin of the word "sheriff."
The eastern part of England where the Vikings settled and Danish law applied.
William's survey of all land and property in England, made for taxation.
Writing about the lives of saints.
A short, sung Celtic tale of love and adventure.
A story of knights on quests, courtly love, and feats of combat.
The 1300s return of Old English-style alliterative poetry.
A medieval play that acts out a Bible story as part of a cycle.
An allegorical play where personified virtues and vices fight for a soul.
A bubonic plague epidemic that killed a huge share of Europe's population.
The change that moved English long vowels to new sounds, so spelling stopped matching speech.
A large manuscript of Old English poems, known for its riddles.
An Old English epic about a warrior hero's battles against monsters.
